paper_b.title: New equidistribution estimates of Zhang type

metadata.description: Both papers attack the bounded-gaps-between-primes problem in the immediate aftermath of Zhang's breakthrough, but via fundamentally different machinery. Maynard (paper A) introduces a multidimensional Selberg-type sieve with weights depending separately on each divisor, eliminating the need for any equidistribution beyond Bombieri-Vinogradov and bypassing Type III estimates entirely. Polymath8a (paper B) instead pushes Zhang's approach by sharpening Type I/II/III equidistribution estimates for primes to smooth squarefree moduli, using the Heath-Brown identity, dense divisibility, q-van der Corput, and the sheaf-theoretic / Deligne machinery for trace-function sums. Their `theorems' overlap only at the high-level goal of improved upper bounds on $H_1=\liminf(p_{n+1}-p_n)$; the technical objects barely intersect.

matches.explanation: Both are the headline theorem of their paper aimed at bounded prime gaps, but they live one level apart in the proof chain. Maynard's TP394.4 ($\liminf(p_{n+1}-p_n)\le 600$) is an unconditional bounded-gap statement obtained through his new sieve; it does NOT require any equidistribution improvement beyond Bombieri-Vinogradov. Polymath8a's TP395.1 is an equidistribution result -- primes equidistribute to smooth squarefree moduli up to $x^{1/2+7/300-\varepsilon}$ -- and is a means to an end (feeding into a GPY-style sieve to produce a bounded gap H_1 in a separate Polymath paper). They are analogous as `the main theorem of the paper that yields bounded gaps' but the mathematical content is on different sides of the sieve/equidistribution divide.

Maynard's $\liminf(p_{n+m}-p_n)\ll m^3 e^{4m}$ for all $m$ is a contribution unique to the multidimensional sieve approach: large $k$ + the $M_k\gtrsim\log k$ asymptotic delivers many primes in bounded intervals, not just two. Polymath8a says nothing about $m\ge 2$ gaps; that lies entirely outside the equidistribution program.
Theorem 1.2 (positive proportion of admissible $m$-tuples satisfying the prime $m$-tuples conjecture) is a counting consequence specific to Maynard's sieve. Polymath8a has no analogue.

The Elliott-Halberstam-conditional bounds $\liminf(p_{n+1}-p_n)\le 12$ and $\liminf(p_{n+2}-p_n)\le 600$ are conditional outputs of the multidimensional sieve. Polymath8a does not assume EH and treats it only as a target-style hypothesis on level-of-distribution; no conditional gap statement appears.

Both papers cite the same classical Bombieri-Vinogradov theorem as external prior work (origin: external in both JSONs). Maynard's TP394.1 is the standard PNT-on-AP form; Polymath8a's TP395.4 is the bilinear (Bombieri-Friedlander-Iwaniec) form. The underlying input is the same, but each paper invokes the variant suited to its machinery (Maynard needs only level $1/2$, Polymath8a needs the bilinear smoothness).

Maynard explicitly invokes the Elliott-Halberstam conjecture as a hypothesis for Theorem 1.4. Polymath8a never states EH as a node; its level-of-distribution improvement TP395.1 ($1/2+7/300$) is precisely what one would push toward EH, but EH itself is not a node in the JSON. Listed as a none for completeness on Maynard's side.

Both define `level of distribution' style quantities for the primes. Maynard's DP394.2 is the classical scalar level-of-distribution $\theta$ for $\Lambda$ in arithmetic progressions. Polymath8a's DP395.6 packages the same idea in much finer form -- Type I/II/III estimates indexed by $(\varpi,\delta,\sigma)$ over moduli with multiple dense divisibility. Same role (controls how far one pushes equidistribution to AP) but very different formal statements.

The notion of admissible $k$-tuple is fundamental to the sieve side and is only invoked in the GPY-type sieve that consumes Polymath8a's equidistribution output (in a separate paper). The Polymath8a JSON does not contain admissibility as a node.
The prime $k$-tuples conjecture is referenced by Maynard as the conjectural target. Not present in Polymath8a (whose target is equidistribution, not the conjecture itself).

The multidimensional Selberg-type sieve weights $\lambda_{d_1,\ldots,d_k}$, the sums $S_1,S_2$, and the smooth-$F$ parametrisation are the central technical innovation of Maynard. Polymath8a uses a different sieve apparatus (Type I/II/III bilinear estimates on the $\Lambda$ convolution) and contains no analogue.
The functionals $I_k(F),J_k^{(m)}(F)$, the maximal ratio $M_k$, the simplex $\mathcal{R}_k$, and the smooth-$F$ ansatz are all tied to Maynard's variational approach. No counterpart in Polymath8a.
Change-of-variables to $y_{r_1,\ldots,r_k}$ and $y^{(m)}_{r_1,\ldots,r_k}$ are internal to the Maynard sieve manipulations (Lemma 5.1-5.3). Not relevant to Polymath8a.
Asymptotics for $S_1,S_2$ (Maynard's Main Proposition 4.1) is the heart of the Maynard sieve evaluation. No analogue in Polymath8a.
Proposition 4.2 (explicit gap statement: positive proportion of admissible tuples yield $r_k$ primes among $n+h_i$) is sieve-side only.
Lower bounds $M_5>2$, $M_{105}>4$, $M_k\gg\log k$ are variational/ numerical facts about Maynard's functional. No analogue in Polymath8a.
Proof of Maynard's Proposition 4.2. No counterpart object on the Polymath8a side.
Deduction of Theorems 1.1-1.4 from Propositions 4.2, 4.3 is Maynard-specific.
Selberg sieve manipulations (Lemmas 5.1-5.3) expressing $S_1,S_2^{(m)}$ in $y$-variables are entirely inside the Maynard sieve and have no Polymath8a counterpart.
Asymptotics of $S_1$ and $S_2^{(m)}$ under the smooth $F$ choice (Lemmas 6.2, 6.3). Internal to Maynard.
Beta-function / quadratic-form lemmas (7.1, 8.1) used in Maynard's evaluation of $M_k$. No analogue.
Proofs of Proposition 4.3 (large $k$ asymptotic and small $k$ generalized eigenvalue computation). No analogue in Polymath8a.

Paper-original examples (admissible 5-tuple, set of $k$ primes) used in deductions. Not L1 contribution-level matches but are paper-origin, listed for completeness on the L1 side. (Note: by §Compactness rules, examples are exempt from `none' requirements; included here only because they are paper-origin and load-bearing for Maynard's deductions.)

Multiple dense divisibility $\mathcal{D}^{(i)}(y)$ is a Polymath8a innovation enabling iterated $q$-van der Corput. No analogue in Maynard, who works with smooth-$F$ weights free of any divisibility structure beyond the standard Selberg sieve.
The Siegel-Walfisz property and located coefficient sequences are Polymath8a-side bookkeeping for the bilinear bounds. Maynard does not enter this framework.
Polymath8a's discrepancy $\Delta(\alpha;a(q))$ is the central quantity bounded in MPZ/Type estimates. Maynard does not appeal to discrepancy in this form.
Squarefree set with prime factors in $I$ and the product $P_I$ are technical conventions used in Polymath8a to handle moduli; not present in Maynard.
MPZ$^{(i)}[\varpi,\delta]$ and the Motohashi-Pintz-Zhang theorem are the equidistribution backbone of Polymath8a. Maynard's program sidesteps this entirely.
New Type I/II/III estimates: the heart of Polymath8a's improvement over Zhang. No analogue on the Maynard side -- Maynard's improvement bypasses Type III altogether.
Combinatorial trichotomy decomposing the convolution into Type 0/I/II/III, and the reduction MPZ -> Type I+II+III: Polymath8a-specific.
Properties of dense divisibility (lcm closure, smoothness, etc.) -- Polymath8a-specific.
Properties of convolved coefficient functions $\alpha_k$ from the Heath-Brown decomposition. Internal to Polymath8a.

Exponential sum machinery (CRT, fundamental theorem of calculus mod $q$, two-modulus sums, Polya-Vinogradov, Ramanujan-Weil, incomplete additive character sums, dense-divisibility-aware vdC corollary) is central to Polymath8a. None of this appears in Maynard.
Reduction-to-$\Upsilon_{\ell,r}$ exponential-sum estimates feeding the Type I/II refinements. Polymath8a-specific.

No-polynomial-phase invariance theorem, the two-pole rational kernel bound, and the incomplete trace function vdC bounds are deep Polymath8a contributions building on Deligne / sheaf theory. Outside Maynard's scope.
Hyper-Kloosterman correlation lemmas. Polymath8a-specific.
Sato-Tate over short ranges for composite moduli: a Polymath8a-side equidistribution result for Kloosterman angles.
New Type III estimates -- Polymath8a's most technical theorem. Maynard's framework explicitly avoids needing any Type III input.

Diagonal/off-diagonal sums, radical-weighted Euler series, GCD sum estimates, and the clean-up factorisation for $\Psi(d,n+dl)$ are technical Polymath8a-side lemmas in the Type III and improved Type I reductions.
Bound on $\Upsilon_4$ (improved Type I) and the two-variable van der Corput proposition (`lode'). Polymath8a-specific.
